title: Common Law and Juries
objective: After this level you can explain how common law and trial by jury developed.
summary: Under Henry II the king's courts built a common law for all England. His Assize of Clarendon (1166) created juries that named suspects; after 1215 juries also decided guilt.

cards.headline: The first English juries didn’t decide who was guilty. They named suspects.
cards.body: Under Henry II, twelve local men were the king’s informers. How did a jury go from pointing fingers to deciding cases? The answer runs through 1215.

cards.headline: One law for all England
cards.body: Henry II, king from 1154 to 1189, sent royal officials around the country to look into how justice was being done. Out of the king’s courts grew common law: law common to all England, instead of a patchwork of local customs. Judges came to follow earlier decisions as precedent, so each ruling guided the next. Think of a family recipe book: nobody wrote it in one go, but every cook adds a page.

cards.headline: Twelve men of the hundred
cards.body: In 1166 Henry’s Assize of Clarendon told each hundred, a district of a county, to pick 12 men (and each township 4) to report crimes and name suspects to the king’s travelling judges. This jury decided who should be accused, not who was guilty. It was the ancestor of today’s grand jury. Picture a neighbourhood watch with the king’s judges on speed dial.

cards.headline: From accusers to deciders
cards.body: Then, in 1215, the Church pulled its priests out of trials by ordeal (Level 74 has the gory details). England needed a new way to settle guilt, and it had a group of sworn neighbours ready: the jury. Soon juries were deciding guilt as well. On the continent, Level 5’s Justinian code became the root of civil law. England went its own way, and its common law later spread to the United States and most of the Commonwealth.

cards.headline: Common law and juries: known
learned: Henry II’s courts built a law common to all England
Judges followed earlier decisions as precedent
1166: juries named suspects to the king’s judges

questions.prompt: Under the Assize of Clarendon in 1166, what did Henry II’s juries do?

options.label: Chose the next king whenever the old one died
options.rationale: They dealt with crimes, not crowns.

options.label: Carried out ordeals by hot iron and cold water
options.rationale: Priests ran ordeals; juries reported crimes.

options.label: Collected the taxes for the king’s wars in France
options.rationale: That was a matter for Parliament, later.

options.label: Reported crimes and named suspects to the king’s judges

questions.explanation: Juries of 12 men from each hundred reported crimes and named suspects to the travelling judges; they didn’t decide guilt.

questions.prompt: Why is England’s medieval common law called “common”?

options.label: It was made up by common people, not kings
options.rationale: It grew in the king’s own courts.

options.label: It was law common to all England, not local custom
It covered only common, everyday crimes
options.rationale: It covered the whole realm’s law.

options.label: It copied the laws of the Roman Empire
options.rationale: That describes civil law, not common law.

questions.explanation: Common law was law common to the whole of England, built from the king’s courts rather than local customs.

questions.prompt: Level 5’s Justinian code became the root of civil law. What was England’s common law built from instead?

options.label: A commission of lawyers that sorted old Roman law
Decisions of the king’s courts, followed as precedent
The rules written for Benedict’s monasteries
options.rationale: Monastic rules governed monks, not the realm.

options.label: A code written by Parliament in 1295
options.rationale: Common law came from judges’ decisions, not one code.

questions.explanation: Common law grew from the decisions of the king’s courts, which later judges followed as precedent.
